also: would you like to take a stroll?

evidence: Cic. Fin. 5.47: quem ad modum quis ambulet, sedeat (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The everyday verb for walking, as against sitting, standing or running, and for walking about for exercise. “Go for a walk” is the supine with īre: ambulātum īre (Cic. Leg. 1.14, as Lewis & Short reads it), deambulātum īre (Cato in Cic. de Or. 2.256).

terms.gloss: go on foot, walk (not ride or drive)
evidence: Cic. Sen. 34: cum ingressus iter pedibus sit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Also pedibus venīre, proficīscī: on foot, as against on horseback or by carriage.

terms.gloss: walk up and down, pace about

terms.comment: Rare (Lewis & Short). Short de- before a vowel, as Lewis & Short marks it (dĕambulo), against Traupman’s dēambulāre.

evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 59: cum resideret, deinde spatiārētur (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: nam ut tibi ambulandum, ungendum, sīc mihi dormiendum.
phrases.english: for as you must walk and oil yourself, so I must sleep.

phrases.latin: Sōcratēn ferunt, cum ūsque ad vesperum contentius ambulāret quaesītumque esset ex eō quārē id faceret, respondisse sē, quō melius cēnāret, obsōnāre ambulandō famem.
phrases.english: They say that when Socrates was walking hard until evening and was asked why he did it, he answered that he was buying in hunger by walking, so as to dine better.
Get ready, so that we can go for a walk.
Would you like to take a stroll?
Then my friends and I go for a walk.
